Hi, Doctor. Well, my manager actually told me I needed to come in. I’ve been waitressing at this diner for a few years now, ever since I took a break from college. It was supposed to just be a semester but you know how that goes, you just keep working to pay the bills. Anyway, it gets really busy during the lunch rush, and usually I am great at it, I can balance like four plates on one arm and keep everything straight. But lately... I don't know, things just haven't been clicking right. 

What really scared everyone at work, and honestly it kind of freaked me out too when my manager pulled me aside about it, is that I started just... freezing up in the middle of service. Like, totally stopping in my tracks. Or I would start doing things completely out of order. There was this one shift recently where apparently I was just standing over by the soda station for I don't even know how long. I was just standing there holding the cash drawer key, which I wasn't even supposed to have right then, and I was just repeating table numbers out loud. Just saying table four, table seven, table nine, over and over again instead of actually closing out my checks like I was supposed to be doing. 

My coworker had to literally take the key out of my hand because customers were waiting to pay, and I just... I didn't even realize I wasn't doing my job. It is just so much pressure and my brain just kind of gets stuck on a loop, I guess? And my manager said I couldn't come back on the floor until I got checked out because it is a liability or something, which is so frustrating because I really need the tips right now, my rent went up again and... yeah, so that is why I am here.

Guilty? Um... no, I don't think so. But lately, I just... I don't feel it. I just go get the ranch and hand it to them, and that's it. There's no guilt, no remorse, no feeling bad about it. It's just another thing that happens, and then it's over. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel guilty about anything. It's just more of that... blankness, I guess.

Well, yes, I suppose that goes right back to what I've been saying, doesn't it? It's all tied together. The pleasure, the joy... it's just not there. Like I was saying about the beach walks and the sea glass. I used to feel this... this little thrill, you know? When the sun would hit a piece of glass just right in the sand, and it was that perfect, frosted blue color. I'd pick it up and rub it between my thumb and forefinger, and I'd feel this little burst of happiness, this sense of finding a tiny treasure. It was joyful. But now, even if I did force myself to go to the beach—which I don't, I don't really go for beach walks anymore at all—but if I did, and I saw a piece of blue glass, I wouldn't feel anything. I wouldn't care. It would just be a piece of trash in the sand to me now. 

And the baking, too. I mentioned the smell of the sourdough filling the apartment. That used to bring me so much pleasure. Taking that hot, crusty loaf out of the Dutch oven and hearing it crackle as it cooled on the wire rack... that was pure joy for me. The anticipation of cutting into it and seeing the crumb structure, of tasting that first slice with a little bit of salted butter melting into it. But I don't bake anymore. I don't have the starter. And even if someone handed me a fresh, warm loaf of sourdough right now, I don't think I'd get any pleasure out of eating it. It would just be food. Just something to chew and swallow. 

It's the same with the gardening, not that I do that anymore either. Seeing a new leaf uncurl on my Monstera plant used to make my whole morning. Now, the plants are dead, and I feel nothing. And my journal... I haven't written in it in I don't know how long. I used to love the feeling of the pen scratching across the paper, getting all my thoughts out, organizing my mind. It was satisfying. Now, the thought of picking up a pen just feels... pointless. 

And, you know, I keep bringing up my husband, but it's true there, too. When he comes home and tries to talk with me, I mostly just sit there. I used to enjoy our evenings together, hearing about his day, telling him about the crazy customers at the diner, laughing about things. That connection used to bring me a lot of joy. But now, when he's talking, it just feels like... noise. It feels like I can't get myself to care about what he's saying, or start a conversation, or even initiate anything at all. The joy, the pleasure, the satisfaction... it's all just completely gone. It's like the part of my brain that registers those good feelings has just shut down completely.

Hurting myself? Um... no. No, I haven't had any thoughts like that. Honestly, I think that would require a lot more energy than I have right now. Like I was just explaining about the blankness and the lack of joy... I feel like you have to feel really strongly about something, like really sad or really desperate or really angry, to want to hurt yourself. You'd have to be in this deep, dark pit of despair. I remember this girl I used to work with at the diner a few years ago, she went through this awful breakup and she would just cry in the walk-in fridge all the time. I don't have any pain to stop, just like I don't have any joy. 

If I wanted to hurt myself, I'd have to actually care enough about my life to want to end it, if that makes sense. I'd have to make a plan and get up off the couch and figure out how to do it, and I just don't have the drive for any of that. It's like the sourdough or the sea glass all over again. Sometimes my husband will leave a knife out on the counter after he makes a sandwich. He makes these turkey and swiss sandwiches for himself in the evenings now since I stopped cooking dinner, and he always leaves the breadcrumbs and the knife just sitting there on the wooden cutting board. And I'll look at it from the couch, and it's just a piece of metal with a handle. It doesn't trigger any dark thoughts or urges or anything. It's just an object taking up space. So no, I'm not sitting there thinking about hurting myself. I'm not really thinking about much of anything, to be honest.

I just sit on the couch. I'm not dwelling on bad memories or feeling hopeless about the future, I'm just... blank. So no, I really wouldn't use the word sad. It's more like the volume on all my emotions just got turned all the way down to zero.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, I guess that’s exactly what I was trying to explain earlier, about the beach walks and the baking and the garden and the journal. Like, I used to get so excited about finding a perfectly smooth, frosted piece of blue sea glass. I had these little glass jars from the dollar store, the ones with the cork stoppers, and I would organize the glass by color—green in one, brown in another, and the rare blue ones in a special little jar on the windowsill so the light would catch them. I loved doing that. It felt so nice. \n\nAnd the baking, oh my gosh, I used to obsess over the crumb structure of my bread. I’d watch all these videos online about hydration percentages and folding techniques, and I’d time my proofs perfectly. It's just another thing that happens, and then it's over. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel guilty about anything. It's just more of that... blankness, I guess.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're unable to experience pleasure from things that normally would bring you joy?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I suppose that goes right back to what I've been saying, doesn't it? How long? Well, I guess... I mean, it didn't just happen overnight, like I woke up one morning and suddenly all the color was drained out of everything. It's been more of a slow fade, I suppose. If I really think back on it, try to pinpoint when things started to shift and get so... flat... I'd say it's been building for about a year and two months. 

Yeah, a year and two months. That's when the manager at the diner, Steve—he's this guy who always wears these really loud Hawaiian shirts even though we're in the middle of the city—he pulled me aside after a lunch rush. I remember it was a Tuesday because we always have the meatloaf special on Tuesdays, and the kitchen was a mess. Anyway, he asked me to take on the evening shift lead responsibilities. At the time, I thought, okay, a little more money, a little more responsibility, maybe it'll be good. But that's really when I started noticing it. At first, it was just feeling a little more tired, a little less interested in chatting with the regulars. I grew cherry tomatoes and sweet basil and mint for tea. And I was always writing in my journal, I have this huge stack of leather notebooks on my nightstand that are just filled up with thoughts and poems and whatever. \n\nBut lately... I don't know. I don't really go for beach walks, bake, garden, or write in my journal much anymore. Actually, not at all. The beach just feels like it's a million miles away, the sourdough starter died months ago because I just stopped feeding it, the plants completely dried up and blew away, and I haven't even opened a pen. It’s not even that I’m actively sad about it, it’s just... I can't get myself to care? Or to start anything. \n\nIt's really affecting things at home, too. Like, my husband will come into the living room and sit down next to me on the couch and try to talk with me. He'll try to tell me about his day or ask what we should do about the groceries or the rent, and I mostly just sit there. I just stare. He'll be talking and I hear the words he's saying, but it feels like there's this heavy, invisible blanket over me and I just can't muster up the effort to respond or participate. I don't feel that sharp ache. I just sit on the couch. I'm not dwelling on bad memories or feeling hopeless about the future, I'm just... blank. So no, I really wouldn't use the word sad. It's more like the volume on all my emotions just got turned all the way down to zero.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, I guess that’s exactly what I was trying to explain earlier, about the beach walks and the baking and the garden and the journal. An intense emotional response? Um... no. No, I really don't. It's like I was saying before about everything just being flat. I don't get those spikes of feeling anymore, not even for a second. 

Like, I remember this one time, maybe two years ago, before all this started. I was walking home from the diner, and I saw this stray cat. It's the same with good things, too. My sister called me last month to tell me she was pregnant with her second baby. With her first, I screamed into the phone, I was so excited. I went out the next day and bought this tiny, ridiculously expensive knit sweater for the baby. But this time, when she told me... I just said, "Oh, that's nice. Congratulations." And I meant it, logically, I know it's a happy thing, but I didn't *feel* happy. There was no surge of joy, no excitement bubbling up. It was just information. 

Even when I drop a plate at work—which happens sometimes, you know, the trays get heavy and the floors get slick by the dish pit—I don't even get that sudden jolt of panic or embarrassment. You know that feeling when you mess up in public and your stomach drops and your face gets hot? I don't get that. The plate shatters, everyone looks, and I just... get the broom. It's completely neutral. There's no spike, no dip, no sudden rush of anything. Just this endless, flat line. So, no, no intense emotional responses at all. Not even for a moment. It's just... quiet. When the sun would hit a piece of glass just right in the sand, and it was that perfect, frosted blue color. I'd pick it up and rub it between my thumb and forefinger, and I'd feel this little burst of happiness, this sense of finding a tiny treasure. It was joyful. But now, even if I did force myself to go to the beach—which I don't, I don't really go for beach walks anymore at all—but if I did, and I saw a piece of blue glass, I wouldn't feel anything. I wouldn't care. It would just be a piece of trash in the sand to me now. \n\nAnd the baking, too. I mentioned the smell of the sourdough filling the apartment. That used to bring me so much pleasure. Taking that hot, crusty loaf out of the Dutch oven and hearing it crackle as it cooled on the wire rack... that was pure joy for me. The anticipation of cutting into it and seeing the crumb structure, of tasting that first slice with a little bit of salted butter melting into it. But I don't bake anymore. I don't have the starter. And even if someone handed me a fresh, warm loaf of sourdough right now, I don't think I'd get any pleasure out of eating it. It would just be food. Just something to chew and swallow. \n\nIt's the same with the gardening, not that I do that anymore either. Seeing a new leaf uncurl on my Monstera plant used to make my whole morning. Now, the plants are dead, and I feel nothing. And my journal... I haven't written in it in I don't know how long. I used to love the feeling of the pen scratching across the paper, getting all my thoughts out, organizing my mind. It was satisfying. Now, the thought of picking up a pen just feels... pointless. \n\nAnd, you know, I keep bringing up my husband, but it's true there, too. When he comes home and tries to talk with me, I mostly just sit there. I used to enjoy our evenings together, hearing about his day, telling him about the crazy customers at the diner, laughing about things. That connection used to bring me a lot of joy. But now, when he's talking, it just feels like... noise. It feels like I can't get myself to care about what he's saying, or start a conversation, or even initiate anything at all. The joy, the pleasure, the satisfaction... it's all just completely gone. It's like the part of my brain that registers those good feelings has just shut down completely.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any thoughts about hurting yourself?\n\nPatient: Hurting myself? Um... no. No, I haven't had any thoughts like that. Honestly, I think that would require a lot more energy than I have right now. Like I was just explaining about the blankness and the lack of joy... I feel like you have to feel really strongly about something, like really sad or really desperate or really angry, to want to hurt yourself. You'd have to be in this deep, dark pit of despair. But I'm not in a pit. I'm just... nowhere. \n\nI remember this girl I used to work with at the diner a few years ago, she went through this awful breakup and she would just cry in the walk-in fridge all the time. She'd talk about wanting to just not be here anymore because the pain was so intense. I remember she dropped a whole tray of milkshakes once and just collapsed right there on the linoleum, sobbing. She was just overflowing with all these terrible, heavy emotions. That makes sense to me, wanting to hurt yourself to make that kind of intense pain stop. But I don't have that. I don't have any pain to stop, just like I don't have any joy. \n\nIf I wanted to hurt myself, I'd have to actually care enough about my life to want to end it, if that makes sense. I'd have to make a plan and get up off the couch and figure out how to do it, and I just don't have the drive for any of that. It's like the sourdough or the sea glass all over again. Sometimes my husband will leave a knife out on the counter after he makes a sandwich. He makes these turkey and swiss sandwiches for himself in the evenings now since I stopped cooking dinner, and he always leaves the breadcrumbs and the knife just sitting there on the wooden cutting board. And I'll look at it from the couch, and it's just a piece of metal with a handle. It doesn't trigger any dark thoughts or urges or anything. It's just an object taking up space. So no, I'm not sitting there thinking about hurting myself. I'm not really thinking about much of anything, to be honest.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been feeling this way, with the lack of interest and emotions?\n\nPatient: How long? Well, I guess... I mean, it didn't just happen overnight, like I woke up one morning and suddenly all the color was drained out of everything. It's been more of a slow fade, I suppose. Just this slow, steady erosion of all the things that used to make me, me. Like I said, it's just chewing and swallowing so my stomach stops making that hollow feeling. I guess I'm eating just exactly enough of whatever is put in front of me to maintain whatever it is I weigh right now, because I'm definitely not getting any bigger, and my clothes aren't falling off me either. No, I don't think so. I haven't noticed anything like that. Traumatic events? Um... no. No, not at all. I mean, I know sometimes people watch those documentaries or read those articles where someone's life falls apart because of some huge, terrible thing that happened to them when they were young, but... no, my life wasn't like that. We moved into our apartment, I started waiting tables... it's just been a very straightforward, quiet life. There's no big traumatic event to point to and say, well, that's why she is the way she is. It's just... nothing. Life was perfectly fine.

That's when the manager at the diner, Steve—he's this guy who always wears these really loud Hawaiian shirts even though we're in the middle of the city—he pulled me aside after a lunch rush. I remember it was a Tuesday because we always have the meatloaf special on Tuesdays, and the kitchen was a mess. Anyway, he asked me to take on the evening shift lead responsibilities. At the time, I thought, okay, a little more money, a little more responsibility, maybe it'll be good. But that's really when I started noticing it. At first, it was just feeling a little more tired, a little less interested in chatting with the regulars. Like, Mr. Henderson would come in for his coffee and pie, and normally I'd ask him about his grandkids, but I just found myself pouring the coffee and walking away. \n\nAnd then it just kept creeping in, you know? The sourdough starter died a few months after that, and then the plants, and then I stopped going to the beach. It's like that promotion, or whatever you want to call it, was the pebble that started the avalanche, except it wasn't an avalanche of feelings, it was an avalanche of... nothing. Just this slow, steady erosion of all the things that used to make me, me. But as far as my clothes go, they all still seem to fit exactly the same. \n\nLike my uniform for the diner... it's this really stiff, black polyester skirt and a white button-down shirt. Like I said, it's just chewing and swallowing so my stomach stops making that hollow feeling. I guess I'm eating just exactly enough of whatever is put in front of me to maintain whatever it is I weigh right now, because I'm definitely not getting any bigger, and my clothes aren't falling off me either. Drugs or alcohol? Um... no. No, definitely not. I've never had any problems with anything like that. 

I mean, working in the restaurant industry, you definitely see a lot of it around you. Like, at the diner, a lot of the line cooks and the other waitresses will go out after a long shift and get absolutely hammered at this little dive bar down the street. The one with the neon martini glass sign in the window that always flickers on the left side. They've invited me a million times over the five years I've been working there. They'll be wiping down the counters at closing and say, "Come on, just come have one beer to take the edge off," but I just... I never really saw the appeal, to be honest. 

Even back when I was taking a few classes at the community college—you know, before I realized that sitting in a lecture hall taking notes wasn't really for me—people would have these house parties and there would be kegs or people passing stuff around. But I just never liked the idea of it. I don't like the feeling of being fuzzy or out of control. And drugs? Definitely not. I don't even like taking aspirin unless I have a really, really bad headache, which I almost never get anyway. 

My husband, he likes to have a glass of wine with dinner sometimes. Usually a cabernet, he buys those specific bottles with the little yellow kangaroo on the label from the grocery store down the street. And sometimes he'll pour me a glass, just trying to be nice, you know, setting it right there next to my water glass. But it usually just sits there on the table next to my plate the entire meal. I don't even take a sip. It just sits there until it gets warm, and then I end up pouring it straight down the kitchen sink when I'm rinsing off the plates. It's just not my thing at all. 

I've never felt the need to rely on anything like that to cope with things or whatever people use it for. It just seems like a waste of money, honestly. And like I was saying before, I don't really have the drive to do much of anything these days anyway, let alone go out of my way to acquire liquor or figure out how to buy drugs. That just sounds exhausting. So, no, absolutely no issues with any of that.
